chapter_theme: Ainkurunuru 91 to 100, the buffalo decade of the marutham hundred (எருமைப் பத்து, Orampokiyar): each short poem opens on a buffalo of the field town, trampling lilies, nursing its calf, resting with its mate, snapping its rope, bathing like a raft or digging up a bather's jewel, and turns to the girl, mostly as the man's praise of the field-lord's daughter, once as the friend's warning that her parents guard her, and once as the complaint of a woman the rope-breaking lord has left sick even by day.

91.reading: The man points out the girl: she is the daughter of the lord of the field town, where the dark curved-horned buffalo bull tramples and tangles the water lilies of the fragrant pond, and she wears a twined garland made from a creeper of the field.
91.nuance: The closing word வெதிர் normally means bamboo, an odd plant for a marutham field and for a garland; what creeper of the field it names cannot be fixed from the line, so the garland's exact material is left open.

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives no thurai; the closing formula (... ஊரன் மகள் இவள்) points to the girl and praises her, which is the man's voice in courtship, telling his companion

thinai_evidence.note: the buffalo, the pond lilies and the field town are all of the watered fields

iraicchi.act: the newly calved buffalo cow gives her flowing udder to the calf she loves
iraicchi.sense: the nursing mother in her father's town is the household of wife and child the man promises if he wins her in marriage

92.reading: The man tells the bright-bangled girl that, if he may have her, he will come to her father's town, where the red-eyed cow of the black-horned buffalo, newly calved, gives her flowing udder to the calf she loves.
92.nuance: 'If we get you' (நின்னையாம் பெறினே) makes the visit a suitor's: to come to the father's town is to ask for her openly, and the nursing cow in that town is the home the asking would found.

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives no thurai; the man addresses the girl directly (ஒண்தொடி மடந்தை நின்னை)

thinai_evidence.note: the field buffalo and its calf belong to the marutham town

93.reading: Because the good buffalo bulls have grazed the fresh red flowers and water lilies bare, the bees, though they have fed their fill of pollen in many groves, now come humming to the crown of this girl's head, where buds are opening.
93.nuance: The grazed field explains the bees' move only on the surface: a reader is meant to hear that the bees, sated on every grove, still choose her flower-dressed hair, the claim the man makes for her fragrance. Line 3 (செய்த இனைய மன்ற) is hard to construe, so how the grazing and the bees are joined is uncertain.

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives no thurai; praise of the girl's hair (இவள் போதுஅவிழ் முச்சி) is the man's voice in courtship

thinai_evidence.note: the buffalo grazing the field flowers is marutham

iraicchi.act: the bull buffalo stays and rests together with his mate in the shaded pool
iraicchi.sense: as the bull keeps beside his mate in her father's fields, the man means to settle with her as husband

94.reading: The man says her father's town, the town of the girl with the bright beautiful forehead where the field lotus blooms, is the one with the shaded pool in the fields where the broad-horned buffalo, like a warrior, rests with his mate, who is like a woman.
94.nuance: The two similes (மள்ளர் அன்ன, மகளிர் அன்ன) make the buffalo pair a man and woman in all but name, so the sense the bull's resting carries lies almost on the surface.

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives no thurai; the closing formula (... ஊரன் மகள் இவள்) points to the girl and praises her, which is the man's voice in courtship, telling his companion

thinai_evidence.note: the buffalo in the field pool and the field lotus fix the watered land

ullurai.tenor: the lord who has slipped the bond of his house and takes his pleasure where he likes

pairs.situation: he has broken the tie that held him to her
he feeds openly in the light of day on what is not his to graze
his open daytime roaming is why her pain comes even by day (பகலும்)

ullurai.speaker_fit: the woman uses the buffalo and paddy of her own town's fields, things she knows (porul 7.26)

95.reading: She says the lord of the water-ringed town, where the black-horned buffalo snaps its rope, ambles off and feeds through the morning on long-eared paddy, has given her, even by day, a hard sickness swollen with longing.
95.nuance: Whether this is the courted girl pining or the wife whose husband has slipped his tether cannot be fixed from four lines; the rope-breaking buffalo, the house's stock image of the straying lord, tilts it toward the second. 'Even by day' (பகலும்) implies the nights were already given over to the pain.

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives no thurai; the sufferer speaks of herself (எமக்கே); the stage, courtship or marriage, is not fixed by the poem

thinai_evidence.note: buffalo grazing paddy in a water-ringed town is marutham

96.reading: This girl, daughter of the lord of the field town, where gem-blue neythal flowers thrive with water lilies in the mire the graceful buffalo wallowed in, is the sweet bed companion of the lord of the pond town.
96.nuance: Two lords are named: her father, the man of the field town (கழனி ஊரன்), and the man of the pond town (பழன ஊரன்) whose bed she shares; to call her his companion of the bed is to declare the union, which is why the speaker is likely the friend making it known to the household. The flowers rising thick from the buffalo's churned mud are scene, not a hidden comparison: they make only one match.

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred and doubtful: the colophon gives no thurai; the girl is pointed out (மகளிவள்) and named the bed companion of a lord spoken of in the third person, which fits the friend disclosing the union to the foster mother better than the man himself

thinai_evidence.note: the buffalo's mire and the field and pond towns are of the watered land

97.reading: The man says this girl, daughter of the lord of the pond town, where the calf of the black-legged buffalo shies at a heap thick with white pakanrai flowers, is more fragrant and cooler than the flowers of the pond itself.
97.nuance: The frightened calf sets a small comic note before the praise; கோட்டை here is a heap or mass of the flowers, which the calf takes for something to fear.

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives no thurai; the closing formula (... ஊரன் மகள் இவள்) points to the girl and praises her, which is the man's voice in courtship, telling his companion

thinai_evidence.note: the buffalo calf and the pond town are marutham

98.reading: The friend tells the lord of the town, where the broad-horned buffalo bathing in cool water looks like a tightly lashed raft, that this bright-bangled young girl's father and mother are stricter with him than she is.
98.nuance: The line concedes that the girl herself would not keep him off; what bars him is her parents' guard, so the only way to her now runs through them, that is, through asking for her in marriage.

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives no thurai; the voice addresses the lord (ஊர) and speaks of the girl and her parents in the third person

thinai_evidence.note: the buffalo bathing in the town's water is marutham

comparisons.tenor: the girl, who relieves his love sickness

99.reading: The man says this broad-shouldered girl, daughter of the lord of the flower-crowded town, where the field buffalo tangles the red-ant nest hanging on the field's bitter-gourd vine together with the ears of grain, has become the medicine for his sickness.
99.nuance: ஆகிய (has become) puts the cure in the past: she is not hoped for as a remedy but has already been one, so the poem stands after their meeting.

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives no thurai; the one whose sickness she cured is the man

thinai_evidence.note: field buffalo, field gourd and grain ears are marutham

100.reading: The man says this girl, daughter of the lord of the prosperous town, where the buffalo digs up on the sand ridge the bright jewel that women bathing in the stream had dropped, has speech sweeter than the strings of the bards' lute.
100.nuance: The buffalo turning up a lost jewel could be read as the man finding her, but that is a single match and stays scene.

links.note: Both set a newly calved buffalo cow beside her calf in the marutham town: in Ainkurunuru 92 the suitor names it as he promises to come for the girl, in Kuruntokai 181 the wife names the same cow, grazing near the calf the ploughman tied, as she speaks of matrons worn by the great house's duties.
links.teaches: The suitor's emblem of the home he offers becomes, in the wife's mouth, the emblem of the home that has used her up, so the one buffalo image measures how courtship's promise of motherhood reads after years of karpu.

links.note: Kuruntokai 2 has the man ask the bee whether any flower it knows is more fragrant than the girl's hair; Ainkurunuru 93 shows bees, already fed full in many groves, coming to hum at her flowered crown.
links.teaches: What Kuruntokai 2 leaves as a question to the bee, Ainkurunuru 93 answers from the bee's own conduct, since a bee sated on every grove that still seeks her hair has given the verdict the lover asked for.

links.note: Both liken the marutham bull buffalo to field warriors (மள்ளர் அன்ன, மள்ளரின்): in Ainkurunuru 94 it rests with its mate in the shaded pool of the girl's father's fields, in Natrinai 260 it leaves the lotus it is tired of and sleeps alone on the sand, in the wife's refusal of the lord.
links.teaches: The same warrior-like bull stands for the husband to come when it stays beside its mate and for the husband who strays when it wanders off sated, so the image's sense in marutham is fixed by whether the beast keeps to its partner, not by its strength.

links.note: Both open on a buffalo that breaks its tether (கயிறுபரிந்து; நோன் தளை பரிந்து) and grazes the town's crops; Akananuru 46 anchors the image in a second marriage over sixteen lines, Ainkurunuru 95 only in 'he gave us a hard sickness even by day'.
links.teaches: That a four-line poem can rest the whole charge on the rope-breaking buffalo, with no wedding named, shows the image was already a fixed sign of the straying lord, which the longer Akananuru poem spells out rather than invents.

links.note: Ainkurunuru 98 has the friend tell the lover that the girl's parents guard her more strictly than she guards herself; Kural 57 asks what use guarding a woman by confinement is, since the guard of her own steadfastness is the best.
links.teaches: The Kural's rule ranks a woman's own guard above confinement, but the Sangam friend relies on the confinement exactly because in courtship the girl's own guard has already given way, so the household's watch the couplet finds useless is what turns a lover into a husband.

links.note: Both say the woman is the cure of the love sickness: Kural 1102 says every other illness has a different cure but hers is cured by herself; Ainkurunuru 99 says the broad-shouldered girl has become the medicine for his sickness.
links.teaches: The couplet's paradox that the cause is the cure is put by the Sangam poem as something that has already happened (ஆகிய), placing the claim after the first meeting, which is where the Kural sets it too, under the joy of union.

links.note: Natrinai 80 has the man, kept away, say there is no medicine but the broad-shouldered girl for his sickness; Ainkurunuru 99 has him say the broad-shouldered girl has become the medicine for it.
links.teaches: The one formula of the girl as the only medicine marks the two ends of courtship, a remedy denied while the friend keeps him off in Natrinai 80 and a remedy received in Ainkurunuru 99, so the tense of the line tells where in the affair the man stands.

source_issues: The colophon of every poem in this decade gives thinai only, no thurai; speakers are inferred from the poems and recorded in thurai_akam with a note.
91 line 1 reads நீலைரும், apparently நீல் இரும் (dark blue-black) written with ை for the sandhi; the sense is clear.
91 line 4 வெதிர் (bamboo) is unexpected for a field creeper used in a garland; the word may be corrupt.
93 line 3 செய்த இனைய மன்ற does not construe easily with what precedes and follows; the line may be corrupt.
99 line 2 writes யெருமை, the glide-initial spelling of எருமை after கழனி.
